title: Ecclesiastes
subtitle: Qohelet's search for gain under the sun, where everything is vapor
lead: Ecclesiastes is the record of one man's search. A teacher who calls himself Qohelet, speaking as a king in Jerusalem, sets out to find what lasting "gain" a person has from all his toil "under the sun" (1:3). He tries wisdom, pleasure, great building projects and wealth, and he watches the world: the oppressed with no one to comfort them, the lonely worker, the king who is forgotten, the righteous who die young. His verdict, repeated about thirty-eight times, is one Hebrew word, hevel: vapor, breath, the mist that is there and then gone. "Vapor of vapors," says Qohelet, "vapor of vapors! Everything is vapor" (1:2).

Yet the book is not only a lament. Seven times Qohelet calls his readers to enjoy life: to eat and drink and see good in their toil, to be glad in what they do, to rejoice in their youth, because these come "from God's hand" (2:24). He teaches that God has made everything beautiful in its time (3:11), that people should fear God and keep their vows (5:1–7), and that the young should enjoy their youth and remember their Creator before old age and death arrive (11:9–12:7). A second voice, a narrator who speaks about Qohelet, frames the book at the start and the end, and closes it by telling the reader to fear God and keep his commands (12:13).

Readers have never agreed about it. Some hear a pessimist who saw through every comfort, some a believer who strips away false hopes so that only God is left, and some a "preacher of joy" who teaches people to receive daily life as a gift. The rabbis debated whether it belonged in Scripture, and Jews read it every year at the Feast of Booths. Christian monks read it as a call to leave the world, and the Reformers read it as a call to do ordinary work gladly before God. This site keeps its key word as "vapor" so that readers can weigh each use for themselves.
facts: Qohelet (קֹהֶלֶת) is a participle from qahal, "assembly": one who gathers or addresses an assembly, or gathers sayings (12:9). Its form is feminine, a form Hebrew uses for offices, so it is probably a title. The Greek translated it Ekklesiastes, from ekklesia, "assembly", which gave the English name Ecclesiastes. "The Preacher" (KJV) comes through Jerome's Latin Concionator and Luther's Prediger, and "the Teacher" is a modern rendering. This site keeps the Hebrew word as a name (see the note at 1:1).

The book calls its speaker Qohelet, "son of David, king in Jerusalem" (1:1; compare 1:12), and from 1:12 to 2:26 he speaks as a king of Solomon's wealth and wisdom, though the name Solomon never appears. Jewish and Christian tradition took Qohelet to be Solomon in his old age (Bavli Bava Batra 15a credits the writing down of the book to Hezekiah and his company). Most scholars today, including many conservative ones, think a later teacher wrote in Solomon's voice, and that a second writer, the frame narrator, added the title (1:1), the refrain at 1:2 and 12:8, the aside at 7:27 and the epilogue (12:9–14).

Traditional view: Solomon, about 970–930 BC. Most scholars: the Persian period (about 450–330 BC) or the early Greek period (about 300–200 BC). The Hebrew is late, close to the Hebrew of the Mishnah; it has many Aramaic words and two Persian loanwords, pardes "park" (2:5) and pitgam "ruling" (8:11). A Dead Sea Scroll copy of parts of chapters 5–7 (4QQoh-a) is dated about 175–150 BC, so the book cannot be later than that.

Judea under foreign rule, a world of trade, money, taxes, officials who watch over officials (5:8) and kings whose favor shifts. The book's literary stage is the court of a wise king in Jerusalem (1:12–2:11). The Temple appears only once, as "the house of God" (5:1), and Israel's history, covenant and prophets are never named.

Wisdom literature in the form of a royal autobiography (1:12–2:26) and a teacher's reflections, mostly in prose, with poems inside it (1:4–11; 3:1–8; parts of 7, 10 and 11; 12:1–7) and many short sayings like those of Proverbs. A narrator frames the whole and speaks of Qohelet in the third person (1:1–2; 7:27; 12:8–14).

Late Biblical Hebrew, with an unusual style: the relative particle she- beside 'asher, many abstract nouns, Aramaic words and two Persian loanwords. Its key words recur again and again: vapor, toil, gain, under the sun, chasing the wind. The Greek translation is very literal, in the style of Aquila. Dominique Barthélemy argued that it is Aquila's own work; most scholars now call it close to Aquila, part of the 'kaige' movement that revised Greek translations toward the Hebrew.

In Jewish Bibles it is one of the Writings and one of the five Scrolls (Megillot), read at the Feast of Booths (Sukkot). In Christian Bibles it stands among the wisdom books, after Proverbs and before the Song of Songs, the order of the Greek Bible.

audience.to: In the book's own voice, students of the wise and a "young man" being taught (11:9; compare 12:1); the epilogue calls its reader "my son" (12:12). Most scholars place the first readers among educated Judeans of the Persian or early Greek period: scribes, officials and merchants in a province ruled by distant kings, who had some wealth and some leisure, knew the confident sayings of Proverbs, and watched the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper.
audience.why: To test the promises of wisdom against what can be seen under the sun, and to teach readers to live honestly inside the limits God has set: no lasting gain, no control over the future, no knowledge of what follows death. What is left is the fear of God, honest speech before him, and the daily gifts of food, drink, work and love, received as a share from God's hand. If, as most scholars think, the book was written for comfortable, thoughtful people who wanted to master life explains its target: not the foolish but the wise, who think wisdom and work can secure their future.
views: Jewish and Christian tradition read the book as Solomon's own reflections in old age, after his turn to other gods (1 Kings 11), written to warn others away from the path he had taken (Targum of Qohelet 1:12; Jerome; many older Christian commentators).

Many scholars hear a teacher in the Persian province of Yehud (about 450–330 BC), where coinage, trade, land grants and royal taxes were new facts of life; Seow argues this from the book's economic words and its Hebrew.

Others date the book to the third century BC, under the Ptolemies of Egypt, when Greek ideas about fate, happiness and the good life were reaching Judea; Hengel and Fox think its questions fit that world, though it has no Greek loanwords. Some scholars hear Greek idioms put into Hebrew, such as "under the sun"; others answer that such phrases are older Near Eastern idioms.

Many think the book comes from a circle of teachers who trained young scribes; the epilogue's praise of Qohelet as one who "kept on teaching knowledge to the people" and its warning about "many books" (12:9–12) suggest a teacher whose students preserved his words.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Qohelet in the settings scholars propose: Persian or early Hellenistic Judea, a scribal school, a world of trade, taxes and officials, with Solomon's court as the book's literary stage (1:12).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was written and edited: its late Hebrew and loanwords, the frame narrator, the epilogue, and the places where Qohelet seems to contradict himself.

lenses.name: Ancient wisdom
lenses.desc: Sets Qohelet beside the wisdom of his neighbors: Gilgamesh and Siduri, the Egyptian harpers' songs, the Babylonian Theodicy, and the Greek thinkers scholars compare.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Follows the book in Jewish reading: the rabbis' debate over whether it belongs in Scripture, the Targum's Torah-centered paraphrase, Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and its reading at Sukkot.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Follows the book in Christian reading: Jerome's commentary, the monks' contempt of the world, Luther's praise of daily work, and modern readings of hevel and joy.

authorship: Jewish and Christian tradition identified Qohelet with Solomon, the only son of David who was king in Jerusalem, and read the book as his reflections late in life, after the Song of Songs and Proverbs (Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1). The Talmud says that Hezekiah and his company wrote the book down (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), meaning they edited or published it. On this view the frame verses (1:1–2; 7:27; 12:9–14) are Solomon speaking of himself, or the work of those who preserved his words. Some evangelical scholars still hold Solomonic authorship, arguing that the late features of the language may reflect a special dialect or later updating of spelling and vocabulary (Archer; Kaiser; compare Fredericks, who argues for an earlier date on linguistic grounds).

Most scholars, including many conservative Jewish and Christian commentators, think the book was written by a sage of the Persian or early Greek period who took on Solomon's role in 1:12–2:26 as a literary device. They point to the late Hebrew, close to the Hebrew of the Mishnah, with Aramaic words and Persian loanwords; to the absence of Solomon's name; and to passages where the speaker views kings as a subject (4:13–16; 8:2–4; 10:16–20). Franz Delitzsch, a conservative Lutheran, wrote in 1875 that if the book were Solomon's, there would be no history of the Hebrew language. Many also see a second voice, the frame narrator, in 1:1–2, 7:27 and the epilogue. Some think one or two later editors added the epilogue, or its last verses (12:12–14), to make the book safer to read (Crenshaw, for example, finds two epilogues, 12:9–11 and 12:12–14). Michael Fox argues the opposite: the frame narrator is the author's own device, a voice through which he presents Qohelet, and the epilogue belongs to the original book.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Ecclesiastes is heavily memorized ('Vanity of vanities', 'a time to be born', 'nothing new under the sun'), and the Plain English Translation keeps familiar wording only where the Hebrew forces it. Most of the book is prose with poems inside it (1:4–11; 3:1–8; parts of 7, 10 and 11; 12:1–7); the poems mark their lines with slashes.

Key terms

Qohelet's style is spare and repetitive on purpose, and the Plain English Translation keeps his repeated words the same each time. Hevel is always 'vapor' ('Vapor of vapors'), never 'meaningless' in some places and 'futile' in others. Qohelet is kept as a name. Re'ut ruach and ra'yon ruach are 'chasing the wind'; ruach elsewhere is 'wind', 'breath' or 'spirit' by context. Tachat hashemesh is 'under the sun', and tachat hashamayim 'under the heavens'. Yitron is 'gain'; 'amal is 'toil', noun and verb; cheleq is 'share'; ma'aseh is 'what is done'; 'olam is 'forever'; miqreh is 'fate', meaning death, the end that meets all. The book never uses the name YHWH ('the LORD'); its word for God is always 'elohim, 'God'. The refrain of joy is rendered the same way wherever the Hebrew is the same; the Hebrew of 2:24 and 3:13 differs a little, so the wording does too ('eats and drinks and sees good in all his toil, it is God's gift', 3:13).

sections.h: Who Qohelet is, and the voice that frames him
sections.b:
The book has two voices. Qohelet speaks in the first person, and for two chapters he speaks as 'king over Israel in Jerusalem' (1:12), describing a life of wisdom, building, wealth and pleasure that matches what 1 Kings tells of Solomon. Another voice speaks about him: in the title (1:1), in the motto 'says Qohelet' (1:2; 12:8), in a brief aside in the middle (7:27) and in the epilogue (12:9–14), which praises Qohelet as a sage who 'kept on teaching knowledge to the people' (12:9), warns against 'many books' and ends with the charge to fear God and keep his commands. Michael Fox called this voice the 'frame narrator'.

Readers have understood the arrangement in several ways. Traditional readers saw Solomon himself, speaking now in the first person and now of himself as 'Qohelet'. Many modern scholars see an author who created Qohelet as a character and frames his words, perhaps with some distance, as a teacher hands on a provocative master's sayings. Others see a disciple or editor who gathered his teacher's words, and perhaps later editors who added the last verses. On any view the frame shapes the reading: the book reports Qohelet's search honestly and then places it within the fear of God.

The Hebrew of Ecclesiastes is unlike that of the books about the kings. It uses the short relative word she- ('that, which') about 68 times beside the older 'asher; it has many abstract nouns (yitron, 'gain'; kishron, 'skill'; holelot, 'madness'); it has words known from Aramaic and later Hebrew ('inyan, 'task'; zeman, 'season'; shabbach, 'praise', 4:2); and it has two Persian loanwords, pardes, 'park' (2:5), and pitgam, 'ruling' (8:11). Many of its words and turns of phrase are otherwise known chiefly from the Mishnah. Most scholars therefore date the book between about 450 and 200 BC. Seow argues for the Persian period from its language and its economic words (money, investment, inheritance, 'gain' and 'share'); Hengel, Fox, Krüger and others prefer the third century BC, when Judea was ruled from Ptolemaic Egypt. The earliest copy, 4QQoh-a from Qumran (about 175–150 BC), sets a latest possible date, and Sirach, written about 180 BC, seems to know the book. A minority defend an earlier date (Fredericks) or Solomonic authorship (Gleason Archer; Walter Kaiser).

sections.h: The shape of the book and its contradictions
sections.b:
No outline of Ecclesiastes has won agreement. The book moves between reports ('I turned and saw'), reflections, proverbs and poems, and returns again and again to the same words. Some scholars have found careful patterns: Addison Wright noted that the book has 222 verses and that the numerical value of the letters of hevel is 37, with 6:9 standing at the midpoint after 111 verses (three times 37). Others think the book is a notebook of linked reflections.

Qohelet seems to contradict himself. He says laughter is madness (2:2) and praises joy (8:15); he hates life (2:17) and says that whoever is joined to the living has something to trust in (9:4); he says God will judge (3:17; 11:9) and that the same fate meets the righteous and the wicked (9:2). The rabbis noticed this (Bavli Shabbat 30b). Explanations include: (1) later pious editors added the orthodox lines (older critics, such as Siegfried); (2) Qohelet quotes common sayings in order to answer them (Gordis); (3) the book is a debate between the voice of faith and the voice of doubt (many traditional readers); (4) the contradictions are deliberate, because Qohelet reports what he observes and the world itself contains them (Fox). Most recent commentators read the book as the work of one mind, wrestling honestly.

The pessimist. Qohelet sees no lasting gain, no justice he can count on, no knowledge of what follows death. His call to enjoy life is a consolation for those who have no other hope. Crenshaw, and in a different way Fox with his 'absurd', read the book as a stark witness to life without guarantees, kept in Scripture because it is honest.

The pious skeptic. Qohelet strips away the false hopes of wisdom, wealth and work in order to leave only God, whose works stand forever (3:14) and who is to be feared (5:7; 12:13). Jerome, the medieval monks and many Reformation and modern evangelical readers (Bartholomew; Iain Provan) take the book this way, as a call to humility before God.

The preacher of joy. R. N. Whybray pointed to the seven calls to joy (2:24–26; 3:12–13; 3:22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:7–12:1) and argued that they carry the book's message: since lasting gain is impossible, receive the daily gifts of food, drink, work and love as God's share for you. Luther read the book much this way.

The frame answers Qohelet. Tremper Longman reads Qohelet as a skeptic whose words the frame narrator quotes in order to answer them. The narrator lets the reader hear the search in full, then in the epilogue turns the reader to the fear of God and the coming judgment (12:13–14). On this reading the book's teaching lies in the frame, not in Qohelet's conclusions.

These readings are not exclusive, and many readers hold more than one of them together.

sections.h: Ecclesiastes beside the wisdom of its neighbors
sections.b: Ecclesiastes belongs to a conversation that ran across the ancient world. In the Old Babylonian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the ale-wife Siduri tells the grieving hero that the gods kept life for themselves and gave death to humans, so he should fill his belly, celebrate, wash, wear clean clothes and delight in his wife and child; Qohelet's 'eat your bread with joy' (9:7–9) is strikingly close (see 9:7–10). Egyptian harpers' songs, sung at banquets, told guests to 'make holiday' because no one returns from death. The Dispute between a Man and his Ba (Egyptian, about 1900 BC) and the Babylonian Theodicy (about 1000 BC) also question whether life and justice make sense. Greek thinkers asked about happiness, fate and the soul, and some scholars find echoes of popular Greek ideas in the book, though it has no Greek loanwords. The parallels show that Qohelet's questions were shared; they do not show that he copied any one source, and his God, who gives and judges, is Israel's.

The rabbis debated whether Ecclesiastes 'defiles the hands', their term for a book that is holy Scripture. The Mishnah records that the school of Shammai said it did not and the school of Hillel said it did (Mishnah Eduyot 5:3), and, with the Song of Songs, it rules that the book does defile the hands. It also records rabbis who disputed Ecclesiastes, and a tradition that the question was decided in its favor on the day Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah was made head of the academy (traditionally at Yavneh, about AD 90–100). Rabbi Akiva said that any dispute had been over Ecclesiastes alone (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5). No council closed the canon there; these are reports of debates among the sages. The Talmud says the sages wanted to 'hide' the book because its words contradict each other, but did not, because it begins and ends with words of Torah (Bavli Shabbat 30b). A midrash says they wanted to hide it because it leans toward heresy, until they read the warning that God will bring every deed to judgment (Leviticus Rabbah 28:1, on 11:9). The Tosefta reports a view that it is not Scripture because it is Solomon's own wisdom (Tosefta Yadayim 2:14). Jerome, who studied with Jewish teachers in Bethlehem, reported that the Hebrews had nearly removed the book and kept it because of its ending. In the end Ecclesiastes was accepted by Jews and by all the Christian churches, though Theodore of Mopsuestia was later reported to have treated Solomon's books as human wisdom rather than prophecy.

Ecclesiastes is one of the five Scrolls (Megillot) read on Jewish festivals: the Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth at the Feast of Weeks, Lamentations on the Ninth of Av, Esther at Purim, and Ecclesiastes at the Feast of Booths (Sukkot), the autumn harvest feast that the Torah calls a time of rejoicing (Deuteronomy 16:14–15). Ashkenazi communities read it publicly on the Sabbath during the feast, a custom first recorded in the Middle Ages; many Sephardic communities do not read it in public. Explanations vary: the book's call to enjoy food and drink as God's gift fits the harvest; its reminder that all is vapor tempers the joy; Solomon dedicated the Temple at this feast (1 Kings 8:2, 65–66). The Targum of Qohelet turns the book toward the Torah and the world to come, and the midrash Ecclesiastes Rabbah reads it as Solomon's teaching about Torah, repentance and judgment.

Early Christian reading was shaped by Origen, who taught that Solomon wrote three books for three stages of the soul: Proverbs for right conduct, Ecclesiastes for seeing through the visible world, and the Song of Songs for union with God. Hippolytus left fragments on the book, Origen's pupil Gregory Thaumaturgus wrote a paraphrase of it, and Gregory of Nyssa preached eight homilies on its first chapters. Jerome's commentary (388/389) grew out of his reading of the book in Rome with Blaesilla, a young widow, to encourage her to despise the world and give herself to God; this 'contempt of the world' became a medieval theme (Bonaventure; the Imitation of Christ, whose first chapter quotes 1:2 and 1:8). Luther, in lectures of 1526, rejected that reading: the book condemns not God's creatures but the restless heart, and it teaches contentment with daily work and gifts. Today Ecclesiastes is read in the Catholic and Revised Common Lectionaries with Jesus' parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21), and its poem of times (3:1–8) is often read at funerals. Christian readers have heard its longing in Paul's words about a creation subject to emptiness and waiting for freedom (Romans 8:20–21): Paul's word, mataiotes, is the word the Greek translation of Ecclesiastes uses for hevel throughout. The New Testament never quotes the book directly, but Christians often read 7:20 with Romans 3:10–12, and the judgment of every deed (12:14) with 2 Corinthians 5:10.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a 'share' when the land was no longer secure
spec.body: My own suggestion: cheleq, 'share', is the word Israel's tradition used for each tribe's and family's allotment of the promised land (Joshua 19:9; Micah 2:4); and when a tribe had no land, as the Levites had none, the LORD himself was their share (Numbers 18:20; compare Psalm 16:5). Qohelet uses it for something much smaller: the enjoyment that comes with food, drink, work and love (2:10; 3:22; 9:9). If the book was written for Judeans in a province where land could be granted, taxed, mortgaged or lost at the pleasure of foreign rulers, and where 'gain' was a merchant's word, Qohelet may be quietly relocating the ancestral 'share' from the land, which no one could hold securely, to the daily gifts of God, which no ruler could take away. Seow and others discuss the economic setting of these words, and commentators note the land background of cheleq; reading it as a deliberate replacement for the land allotment is my own idea, and I have not checked whether a published commentator has made the same argument.

traditions.q: Does Ecclesiastes call Christians to leave the world, or to serve God gladly in ordinary work?
views: Both have a place. The Church has long read the book as teaching contempt of the world's passing goods, the path of monks and religious who leave possessions and marriage (Jerome; Bonaventure; the Imitation of Christ 1.1), while also teaching that ordinary work shares in God's creation and is a path to holiness for laypeople (John Paul II, Laborem Exercens, 1981; Catechism 2427).

The Greek fathers read Ecclesiastes as the second step of the spiritual life: after Proverbs teaches right conduct, Ecclesiastes teaches detachment from visible things, before the Song of Songs leads to union with God (Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes). Monasticism is honored as a high calling, but the same detachment is asked of all Christians in the world.

Luther held that the monks misread the book. It does not condemn the things God made, nor marriage, food or work, but the restless heart that wants more than God gives. Every honest calling, as servant, parent or ruler, is service to God, and the book teaches us to enjoy present gifts with thanks.

Calvin taught a measured contempt for this life compared with the life to come (Institutes 3.9), but insisted that its goods are God's gifts, given for our need and delight, to be used with gratitude and moderation while we work faithfully in our calling, not fled (Institutes 3.10).
